cards.title: Saying no to a senior stakeholder
cards.prompt: Tell me about a time you said no to a senior stakeholder who wanted something on your roadmap.
follow_ups: What did they want, and why did it matter to them?
What did you base the no on?
What did you offer instead?
How did they react, and what happened next?
Would you make the same call today?
strong_answer_covers: Grounds the no in goals, users and data
Offers an alternative path or timing
Keeps the relationship
Clear outcome
Talks to the stakeholder before escalating

cards.title: Moving a team you don't manage
cards.prompt: Tell me about a time you needed an engineering team that didn't report to you to commit to something they didn't want to do.
follow_ups: Why didn't they want to?
What did you change in the plan because of their concerns?
What did you give up to get agreement?
What was the result?
strong_answer_covers: Understands the team's incentives and constraints
Changes the plan based on their input
Agreement built on shared goals, not authority
A measured result
Does not rely on authority or the team's manager

cards.title: A launch that missed
cards.prompt: Tell me about a product or feature you launched that missed its goal.
follow_ups: What was the goal, and how far off was it?
When did you first suspect it would miss?
What did you do about it?
What did you tell leadership, and when?
What do you do differently now?
strong_answer_covers: A clear, measured goal and the gap
Owns the decision, not just the execution
Acted on the miss: iterated, rolled back or stopped
A lesson visible in later work
Does not blame engineering, design or marketing

cards.title: Deciding without enough data
cards.prompt: Tell me about a decision you had to make before you had the data you wanted.
follow_ups: What data did you have, and what was missing?
What made waiting worse than deciding?
How did you limit the risk of being wrong?
How did it turn out?
strong_answer_covers: Names the missing data and why waiting cost more
Makes the call with stated assumptions
Builds in a way to learn and reverse
Honest outcome
Does not wait for certainty or pretend the data was clear

cards.title: Conflict between design and engineering
cards.prompt: Tell me about a time design and engineering on your team disagreed, and you had to help resolve it.
follow_ups: What did each side want, and why?
What did you do that a manager couldn't have?
How did you decide?
How did both sides feel afterwards?
strong_answer_covers: States both sides fairly
Reframes around the user and the goal
Clear decision and the reason for it
Relationships intact afterwards
Takes a position on the merits, not by who is louder
